title_original: Stacy Kranitz: A Picture Is Worth a Thousand Wounds
excerpt_original: With Ain't No Grave Gonna Hold My Body Down, winner of the Images Vevey Book Award 2025/2026, Stacy Kranitz closes out nearly twenty years of photographing Appalachia. The book and the installation at the Musée Jenisch set her pictures against a century of archives that…

blocks.text: “I don’t believe in ending stories. I just don’t do it.” Stacy Kranitz drops the line by Lake Geneva, on the afternoon of the Images Vevey Book Award ceremony, between two questions about swimming. Seventeen years she has been working in Appalachia, the mountain range that runs more than 3,000 kilometers from Canada down to Alabama. Or twenty, she hesitates. The book takes its title from a gospel song by Brother Claude Ely, a Pentecostal preacher from those mountains. The jury chaired by Rineke Dijkstra crowned it; Éditions Images Vevey and the American publisher Terrible Baby brought it out in June. One idea governs the whole: every image manufactures a little of the reputation it claims to describe.

blocks.caption: Family standing in front of cabin, near Mt. Sterling, North Carolina © Great Smoky Mountains National Park Archive

blocks.text: At the Musée Jenisch, the installation applies that principle to the letter. Stacy Kranitz’s color photographs, made in a West Virginia hollow, face the images produced about the region by outsiders since 1850. Missionaries raising funds, photographers on the payroll of the coal companies, envoys of the Farm Security Administration, reporters covering the War on Poverty: each wave arrived with its commission in hand and its framing already written. And a documentary film directed by the photographer holds the center of the display. “There’s no visual literacy in America,” she says. “Nobody knows, understands, or processes how images circulate in the world, the different kinds of apparatuses that are at play. Nobody thinks about this stuff.”

It all starts on a Friday night in 2013, in West Columbia, West Virginia. Stacy Kranitz is invited for a beer at the home of a man who, within the hour, gets into three fistfights, throws chairs and punches his friend Dozer in the face. On the back of his neck, a tattoo: “Honkey.” The lawyer Harry Caudill would have filed Pat Greene among what he called the “dullards” of the back hollows. The photographer, for her part, keeps coming back for a decade, then another. “To me, he really identifies as a mountaineer,” she says of her host. “He really embodies the idea of living mountain life.”

blocks.caption: West Columbia, West Virginia, 2023, Pat with his daughter Vicky on her birthday © Stacy Kranitz
Photograph of Stacy Kranitz © Sofia Krysiak

blocks.text: One late summer, on a strip mine reclaimed as an ATV trail, Stacy Kranitz climbs on behind Dozer, camera on her back, after a dozen beers for him. The caption of one picture in the book says the rest: “Stacy and Dozer on his four-wheeler, the moment before it flipped.” Dozer, 95 kilos, lands on her; the quad, 340 kilos, lands on Dozer. One bruised elbow. Back at Pat’s, someone hands her a crushed Lortab to snort for the pain. Participant as much as observer, she photographs from inside the circle, with the risks that implies and the standing it earns.

Then comes the long history, the one the book unfolds through documents. Families left Europe to escape a class system, found themselves indentured, climbed into the mountains and lived a century outside capitalism. Then coal climbed up after them. “They literally stole the land,” Stacy Kranitz says. “They didn’t know they needed to have deeds. Nobody told them they need to have deeds. So who decides that they need to have deeds? The coal companies.” On April 24, 1964, Lyndon Johnson sat on the porch of Tom Fletcher, an unemployed miner in Inez, Kentucky, who had earned about 400 dollars the previous year. The picture became the emblem of the War on Poverty. Fletcher died poor in 2004, worn out by the reporters who came back every ten years to ask whether he still was. At the end of the volume, a “lexicon of dispossession” lines up the words coined to keep these people outside the human contract, from waste people to trailer trash . Four centuries of vocabulary, a single function.

blocks.text: Then there is Harry Caudill, the dark heart of the affair and the subject of the film. His essay “The Rape of the Appalachians,” published in The Atlantic in 1962, and Night Comes to the Cumberlands a year later, turned America’s attention to a region bled dry by coal. Twenty years on, the same man explained poverty by genetics, invited the eugenicist William Shockley to his Kentucky home and floated cash bounties for sterilization. Stacy Kranitz unearthed the footage in which he makes that claim on camera. On November 29, 1990, facing Pine Mountain, Caudill shot himself; his farewell letter is reproduced in the book. One detail from the same archive amuses his Swiss publishers. “He mentions the Swiss. He says, we want to do it like the Swiss,” the photographer reports. The film, for its part, turns back on its own author and asks the question that holds for the entire project: what does an image of poverty do, once it is loose in the world?

Next comes J. D. Vance, whose Hillbilly Elegy (2016) recounts an Appalachian childhood and hands his own people the blame for their decline. Stacy Kranitz places the two men in the same frame and notes the coincidence: Pat’s daughter was taken by child protective services just as Vance was named running mate. “It’s my form of politics,” she says of that montage. “I don’t know why we’re not talking about eugenics more. We are still lurking in that conversation in every direction.” A Nieman Fellow, she is spending the year at Harvard, where she studies eugenics and pronatalism.

blocks.caption: Presidential debate between Ohio Senator. J. D. Vance of Ohio and Minnesota Governor. Tim Walz, CBS Broadcast Center, New York, October 1, 2024 © Stacy Kranitz

blocks.text: The book saves its most troubling object for last. In 2016, a photograph of Pat shirtless in his yard became a meme: “Poor southern conservatives have been voting Republican for generations. And they’re still poor.” Pat, with a criminal record, cannot vote. The essayist Whitney Phillips devotes one of the book’s texts to it. Stacy Kranitz has known the mechanism since 2012, when CNN ran her images of a Pentecostal snake handler and a Ku Klux Klan gathering under the headline “Everyday life in Appalachia.” It took a week on the phone to get the headline changed. “Photography has done a lot of harm to that region,” she says. “That doesn’t mean that you can’t or shouldn’t.” She describes the model that governs the news: “A flood, an earthquake, some disaster, we descend on the region, everyone’s there at the same time, and then we abandon ship.” Her work does the opposite, slowly. “Art allowed me to slow down and tell the story over a much longer period of time. You can’t really do it in journalism.”

So she stays. Stacy Kranitz went through every caption with Pat Greene, recorder on the table. “I really needed him to see what I wrote,” she says, “to make sure that he agreed with the context, with the way that it was being used in the book.” The last pictures date from March 2026. As the book went to press, Pat was in jail, with no one to post bail. “We love to put poor people in jail for no good reason,” she says. Five weeks of silence, then a rehab center, where she was able to visit him. “I’ve never seen him more contemplative,” says the photographer, who has always known him in survival mode. The book ends in the dark; life has turned since. Such is the advantage of stories that keep going. “I will probably be there for a long time, and I will not be leaving.”

blocks.text: Ain’t No Grave Gonna Hold My Body Down by Stacy Kranitz is published by Terrible Baby / Éditions Images Vevey and available for $70. The exhibition at the Musée Jenisch, part of the Images Vevey Biennial , runs through September 27, 2026.
